Education within the digital age demands an in-depth analysis of learning processes and concepts, particularly within collaborative learning settings. Curiosity has been identified as a key driver of active engagement and effective knowledge construction, yet there is still a lack of reliable indicators and methodologies for studying its complex nature. This study introduces a pioneering approach to examining curiosity in cooperative learning by fusing emotional and cognitive aspects, leading to a set of multilayered criteria designed to capture curiosity's multivariate essence. These criteria are put to the test in a study on university students working on a challenging science project, resulting in data that reveals the proposed framework can successfully distinguish between varying levels of curiosity. Furthermore, this research outlines specific statistical and machine learning methods for validating and refining cooperation patterns, establishing a robust foundation for future investigations into multilayered emotional phenomena.

Spatial statistical modeling often uses correlation functions that consider a spatial domain's unbounded nature. However, when modeling over restricted areas, like political maps or satellite image covers, alternative approaches are needed. A novel method is proposed that combines a given Gaussian covariance model with a stationary precision matrix to create adaptable long- and short-range correlations within limited regions. The sum of these two components can be reparameterized using a mixture distribution, providing a flexible framework. This framework is explored with prior specifications on parameters that influence both long- and short-range dependencies, demonstrated with applications in simulated and real-world datasets. A challenge arises in ensuring model identifiability due to the competing correlation structures. We address this by addressing the need to avoid double-counting when combining models with similar correlation behaviors. A specific example is the Mat\'ern covariance model, suitable for spatial statistical applications in limited domains. Our approach is illustrated using Mat\'ern Gaussian processes and Gaussian Markov random fields, and the effects of models and prior specifications are analyzed through regression applications.

The design and functionality of intelligent transportation systems depend on accurate maps. Although high-resolution maps exist, creating cost-effective systems to track urban road networks online would be challenging given the scale of the area involved.

A new observation system, comprising mobile sensors on transportation entities, aims to efficiently observe and map urban transportation networks. Initially, this system was intended to track small areas, like business blocks, to verify the accuracy of existing high-resolution maps.

However, with the rapid growth of ridesharing transportation, a system comprising a few hundred mobile sensors can rapidly observe and map entire cities, effectively leveraging transportation entities as sensors to create up-to-date and accurate digital twin maps of urban road networks.

A key consideration in this system is the optimal placement of mobile sensors to ensure comprehensive coverage of the urban road network at a reasonable cost.

We propose a novel approach, called Road-system Detection Optimization, to efficiently detect entire urban road systems by combining the strengths of index-based formulation and iterative solution generation.

A case study, comparing satellite imagery, actual sensor data, and a digital twin map of San Francisco, demonstrates the effectiveness of this system and outperforms a previous approach, including significantly reducing computational time.

J/psi decays into visible photons and any invisible particles present will have far-reaching implications, as they signify modifications to the Standard Model electroweak theory at the scale of the J/psi mass. These scales are remarkably close to the effective field theory match point for neutrinos, as well as for the J/psi scale's remainder dark sector and the possible hypothesis of neutrino dark matter.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the 'embedded method' approach, and we extend this work by presenting new variable stepsize SGLMs based on 'assumed form' techniques. For both types of methods of order $p$ and $q$ ($p \geqslant q$), we establish convergence conditions and provide error bounds. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our SGLMs methods are competitive when compared to previously established variable stepsize methods for solving second order initial value problems.

This document multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) is introduced, building on the components of univariate functional singular spectrum analysis (USSA). It covers the decomposition of multivariate functional time series, reconstruction methods, and component-specific considerations, namely library selection, missing data handling, and component-wise features. To demonstrate the procedure, two applications are examined: atmospheric circulations and their associated heatmaps and the multivariate functional time series of NFL team performances. Furthermore, the document also includes the algorithm for implementing multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis.

In contrast to traditional frameworks that emphasize fairness across all individuals, assurance frameworks are designed to guarantee a minimal level of fairness. Recently, these types of frameworks have gained significant popularity due to their ability to balance efficiency and fairness while ensuring inclusivity for underrepresented groups. Nevertheless, recent studies have highlighted the inherent instability of such frameworks, indicating susceptibility to both subtle forms of manipulation as well as more substantial attacks. This study delves into the underlying issues that give rise to these problems with the assurance approaches, investigating their effects on the algorithms' outputs as well as the structural characteristics that contribute to their vulnerability. We present an in-depth examination of the assurance frameworks' limitations, including multi-objective optimization models, cooperative games, and decision-support systems that incorporate fairness constraints. To further facilitate understanding of these issues, we introduce the AES assurance frameworks analysis toolkit, which provides researchers with the ability to investigate fairness issues associated with various models and settings. Through this framework, we explore the sensitivity of multi-objective optimization models to subtle manipulations, demonstrate how constraint-based approaches can be susceptible to both subtle and substantial attacks, and analyze the impacts of both types of attacks on the core values of AESs within decision-support systems. Ultimately, our research offers valuable insights that may assist in addressing the over-sensitivity of assurance frameworks through alternative designs, including the use of non-linear constraints, sequential optimization, and diverse evaluation metrics.

The study of one-dimensional Brownian motion and its discrete counterparts, such as simple symmetric random walk, has been extensively documented in comprehensive survey articles, particularly those by Salminen, Vostokov, and Zholudjev, as well as by Geman, Overall, and Patie. Our research focuses on filling knowledge gaps in the existing literature by examining the duration that a random walker spends in an arbitrary state within a specified time frame. We investigate under which conditions on boundary functions of open intervals, the probability of at least one occurrence of the interval's midpoint during the given time frame approaches a non-zero value. Establishing this condition, we derive explicit expressions for persistent probabilities of constant and exponential functions, calculating their values for a range of given times.

This study seeks to clarify the previously ambiguous region of operation for h/I~0~ in the IShTAR plasma generator. A detailed analysis of plasma parameters was conducted in various regions, including near wall, mid ramp, and mid coil. Data were collected after reaching plasma steady state. A plasma generator design was optimized using insights gained from this analysis. A specific focus of the study lies in exploring the described helicon regime in greater depth. A model was used to explain the transition from cyclist to helicon mode, and criteria for this transition were derived. A plot of these criteria successfully delineates the two distinct regimes. Furthermore, analysis of power distribution in plasma revealed that a distinct shift occurs when crossing from cyclist to helicon mode. This shift is clearly marked by a change in how plasma is heated. A predicted increase in plasma density was also confirmed by experimental evidence.

To mitigate disease transmission, several strategies exist, including personal protective measures and using safe, effective microbial biopesticides. In this study, we aim to model the impact of microbial biopesticides on disease transmission. We present a Lagrange formulation to analyze the suppressing effect of a biopesticide on a food web model that incorporates the biopesticide. Furthermore, we present the results of our investigation through an example model featuring a mycopathogen for controlling the pink-sugar aphid, a significant agricultural pest.

Malignant disease detection via histopathology image analysis has significant clinical implications, but its effectiveness relies on accurate nucleus detection, segmentation, and classification, which are hampered by obstacles including varying image scales, color, extensive nucleus counts, and close-proximity positioning, preventing clinicians from manually identifying all nuclei in the images, necessitating the development of an automated system for nucleus detection and classification. While previous research efforts have made considerable progress, nucleus detection and classification remain challenging tasks. To tackle this, we propose a novel, unified framework for histopathology image nucleus detection and classification, which incorporates a two-stage network comprising a coarse detector and a refined classifier, and introduces a novel approach to nucleus classification, and introduces a novel approach to nucleus classification via feature domain adaptation, allowing for the efficient utilization of data from multiple classes, and introduces a novel approach to nucleus classification via feature domain adaptation, allowing for the efficient utilization of data from multiple classes.

Furthermore, to address the discrepancy in nucleus distribution across multiple classes, we propose a novel approach to nucleus classification via feature domain adaptation, which leverages a generative adversarial network to learn a shared feature representation, and introduces a novel approach to nucleus classification via feature domain adaptation, which leverages a generative adversarial network to learn a shared feature representation, and introduces a novel approach to nucleus detection via feature domain adaptation, which leverages a generative adversarial network to learn a shared feature representation, and introduces a novel approach to nucleus classification via feature domain

We establish a novel application for the Fourier transform of a distribution, and a key identity achieved by Casselman and Nelson, for certain types of groups (odd symplectic and orthogonal) in $GL_n(k)$, where $n$ is either 2m-1 or 2m, and $k$ is a complex number. Notably, we utilize this framework to simplify the derivation of a special case of the converse theorem for these types of groups, and our method is distinct from previous approaches that depended on the groups being redexial.

This paper defines two new graph properties: a graph G is considered to have a certain hamiltonian cycle characteristic if its n-th iterated line graph contains a hamiltonian cycle or route for all positive integers n, and we also define graphs with n-th iterated line graph being hamiltonian path/cycle connected or bipartite in the same manner. The purpose of this research is to establish criteria for a graph to have these two specific n-th iterated line graph hamiltonian route/cycle properties.

Epidemiological data indicate rapid worldwide spread of the novel coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Autopsy and radiological findings in coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) severe cases showed extensive pulmonary inflammation. Moreover, laboratory discoveries of SARS-CoV-2 in deceased severe COVID-19 patients' lung macrophages pointed to pyroptotic cell death as a possible cause of cytokine storm. Building on the characteristics of SARS-CoV-2, including the activation of caspase-1 and the inhibition of autophagy, we developed a solitary-cell model to examine cellular processes during pyroptosis. Using this model, we explored the dynamics of cellular components and pyroptotic cell death, and confirmed our theory through a match with experimental data on the effects of sarin exposure and rapamycin administration. Furthermore, the model can help design effective anti-inflammatory treatments for severe COVID-19 patients.

External influences that affect a task can hinder learning by other agents and generate misleading signals. Identifying and removing these external factors, including variables and sources of reward unrelated to the agent's actions and state, can streamline the learning process. We propose a method to eliminate such factors, making the reward dependent solely on the agent's control of endogenous state variables. This approach allows the agent to focus on learning from relevant signals. We evaluate our method and propose an alternative, using reinforcement learning. It is shown that our method can successfully remove extraneous information and facilitates efficient learning, particularly for humans. Moreover, we introduce a theoretical explanation for our method and an alternative using Bayesian inference.

Consensus-based blockchain platforms utilize smart contracts to execute agreements, but their secure implementation poses a significant challenge. This work introduces a validator based on refinement types for a subset of Coq, specifically tailored to the Syntactic Michelson language. The validator ensures the precise and intended computation of Michelson programs, and can be employed to create a reliable refinement of Michelson by integrating it with a refinement monad. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated in a case study on transferring funds within the Tezos blockchain.

Due to their effectiveness, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are widely utilized for advanced applications, but their success relies heavily on input features being preprocessed appropriately. In contrast to conventional CNNs, which can be trained independently of feature preprocessing, GCNNs necessitate a careful consideration of a trade-off between bias and variance. This is because features are transformed both by an explicit method and a hidden layer within the network. Moreover, we've identified that the core function of GCNNs' message passing layers is statistically equivalent to a matching filter, which optimizes feature estimation by minimizing estimation errors. This filter is further optimized to balance feature estimation efficiency and variance, ensuring convergence as the number of preprocessing steps plus input dimensions increases. Since GCNNs are essentially composed of multiple such matched filters in sequence with varying optimization goals and parameter sets, we propose a flexible framework that allows for a clear comprehension of GCNN behavior. Through this framework, along with supporting mathematical proofs and experimental analyses, we highlight crucial factors that influence GCNN performance and provide a valuable tool for predicting biases introduced by feature preprocessing methods.

A scalar field self-interacting through a $\lambda\phi^4$ term is made to rotate around the z-axis in equatorial flat space, which results in a source term representing a symmetric, traceless tensor. The path integral of this term, integrated over a Chern-Simons action of this tensor and its corresponding gauge field at high-dimensional boundaries, produces a non-trivial boundary Chern-Simons theory. A dual supergravity model is then developed for this boundary theory, yielding a unique solution that represents a black hole with hair, characterized by non-zero angular momentum and mass arising from this interaction, while remaining massless in the absence of this boundary term, even with non-zero angular momentum. A corresponding soliton solution is also found, which describes a solid body of this hairy matter in rotation, reaching its extremum at maximum angular velocity, where its mass and angular momentum both equal zero, with the interior rotating at varying angular velocities and accumulating matter at the equator in a density determined by this boundary term.

Although membranes and higher-dimensional objects have been extensively studied in theories containing fermions, the understanding of non-reversible symmetries like chiral and super-symmetric invariance was limited. This research introduces a generalized world-volume action that encompasses all possible supersymmetric invariances, including the W-invariance in odd-dimensional spaces where fermions are present. The complex super-field theoretical structure of this action was previously difficult to manage, but a key advancement has been the introduction of a specific super-coordinate transformation that simplifies the application of the W-invariance principle. Furthermore, a notable outcome of this research is the identification of all possible locally super-symmetric invariances present within a given odd-dimensional space based on the number of supercharges available.

In Traditional CSA-based methods for ultrasound elastography, accurately estimating the shift in the cross-sectional direction is challenging due to errors caused by interpolation when using Cartesian coordinates. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach known as Virtual Origin CSA (VOCSA) has been proposed for phase correlation elastography, where the radial coordinates are extended to cover a broader range and then mapped to a Virtual CSA (UCSA) coordinate system with a reduced range. USCX coordinates corresponding to the original UCSA locations allow researchers to analyze elastography data in CSA format without excessive interpolation, thereby minimizing spatial and temporal errors. Both VOCSA and CSA simulations have demonstrated the superiority of the novel approach in providing more accurate lateral displacement measurements, with improvements of approximately 0.2 pixels (equivalent to around 50 micrometers at a 0.3 millimeter axial pixel size).

Algorithms are often represented using formal or informal pseudocodes, which have a long-standing role in computer science education and analysis. Despite the widespread practice of associating codes with program executions or demonstrations to improve comprehension, research on learning from examples has primarily focused on syntactic reformulations of solutions. Our work suggests a shift towards evaluating the utility of presenting demonstrations of solved problems alongside pseudocodes, and we call this concept "rational pseudocode". To test the validity of this concept, we conduct three experiments involving participants with varying coding backgrounds, where they learn algorithms from either explanatory text alone or from examples alone, and ultimately from pseudocodes, which are optimized for efficiency rather than clarity. Our results indicate that the inclusion of demonstrations significantly enhances the understanding of algorithms through pseudocodes, and that the pseudocodes themselves are capable of effectively conveying complex information.

We explore $V$-posets within the context of Boolean algebras, which are posets formed by pairing two chains of boolean values and ordering them according to a specific structure. Our analysis reveals that within any sufficiently large boolean algebra, there will be a subset that forms a $V$-poset, and further, for any specific coloring, there will be a monochromatic subset that corresponds to a defined $V$-poset shape. Additionally, we identify the exact minimum size of a boolean algebra required to guarantee this property for two particular 'hard-to-find' $V$-posets.

In nearly online settings with repetitive patterns, organizing items into groups serves as a fundamental building block for various optimization problems. Unfortunately, an optimal sequence of groups is sensitive to slight changes, making it impractical to utilize in real-world applications. As a result, researchers have shifted their focus to developing robust solutions that can effectively respond to input changes. Unfortunately, groupings are combinatorial in nature, which has hindered progress in developing dynamic algorithms that consider cost efficiency and sensitivity simultaneously. To address this limitation, we introduce a first-of-its-kind algorithm that uses a more purposeful concept to create nearly optimal dynamic $k$-means solutions that function well in high-dimensional spaces. Our algorithm utilizes a concept called a quasi-optimal sequence to incorporate ideas from sampling and smoothing to achieve an outcome that is within a factor of $\tilde{O}(k^{4.5})$ of the ideal dynamic $k$-means result.

Determining whether repetitive patterns occur in a stochastic pursuit-evasion game on a finite graph is investigated, with the model representing an n-dimensional binary vector where the '1' element signifies the hunter and the '0' elements represent the evader. A predetermined action is executed by the hunter, while the evader responds with either a fixed or alternating sequence of actions, respectively constituting periodic behavior. It is proven that periodic behavior arises from either fixed or alternating actions of the evader, yet almost all pairings of fixed and alternating actions do not result in the emergence of periodic patterns.

Cyclic arrangements hold significant importance in various fields, particularly in statistics, where they are essential for analyzing data that repeats over time. However, standard methods of representing circular distributions can be confusing and yield counterintuitive results. We propose a more straightforward and versatile approach for calculating probabilities in circular settings, which can also be applied to understand nontransitive phenomena. Using simple, real-world examples, we illustrate how our method provides a clearer understanding of situations where elements can be superior to others without being comparable.

Recently, deep learning techniques have made significant advancements, particularly in low-dose CT image reconstruction and the method has been eliminated from the 2019/2020 ACROP denoising challenge. Due to its supervised nature high dose images to low-dose images, a few unsupervised learning methods have been proposed, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), which learn mapping from unsupervised low-dose images to the true high-dose images. In this paper, a new unsupervised learning approach, called AdaLN-Switching Low-Dose CT (ACGP), is introduced to address the issue of no pairing of high-dose and low-dose images. This method allows the generator network to create multiple distinct styles from a single latent code, which can be controlled by adjusting the normalization parameters of each branch. The AdaIN module is employed, which enables the use of high-dose images as reference for each branch, thereby guiding low-dose images to different high-dose image styles. During training, only one branch is employed at a time, and the model selectively uses low-computation power to normally train. The proposed AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN method is verified on the publicly available low-dose CT dataset, which includes 147 cases, and the results indicate significant improvements, which outperform existing unsupervised methods by a 10 dB ISEE metric on average.

Recent dialogual language understanding models have achieved significant success thanks to pre-training techniques that utilize vast amounts of internet data. However, dialogues are complex due to their multi-turn nature and unique characteristics, such as multi-hop reasoning, long-distance dependency, and context pruning, which are not fully captured by current conversation sources. To address this, we introduce SPACE-2, a new pre-training framework for tree-structured language understanding that combines contrastive learning and involves three main components: generating contrastive learning samples, extracting useful information, and generating conversational head units through these components. We evaluated SPACE-2 on the STREUCOMpile dataset for event argument extraction and the DialogState Tracking task, obtaining state-of-the-art results in both tasks with few additional training parameters. Furthermore, we present a dialog state tracking task-specific version of the pre-training framework called SPACE-2+.

This research focuses on establishing the structure and form of a ideal fluid cosmology, assuming its metric forms a conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton, and ultimately proving a key theorem regarding this type of cosmology.

Recent measurements of spin alignment in distorted halo nuclei have revealed unexpected patterns that do not match expected results. To to address this, theoretical calculations were performed to explore possible explanations. Notably, calculations show that spinning a distorted core significantly impacts the overall shape of a halo nucleus, leading to unexpected increases in spin alignment for certain nuclei like $^{11}$Be, $^{19}$Na, and $^{29}$Na. However, this effect is observed to an extent that it would manifest as minimal alignment for $^{11}$Be. Moreover, potential explanations are provided for recent experiments involving the transfer of a halo neutron to a rotating nucleus, showing how the occurrence of coupling between the shape and spin could result in alignment values lower than those predicted.

We introduce BasicVSR++, an advanced version of the BasicVideo Super-Resolution model, that overcomes the limitations of the original and other mainstream methods. To achieve this, we utilized high-resolution guidance in both forward and backward processes to minimize inaccurate pixel mapping, as well as employed channel mixing layers to capture long-range dependencies, thereby improving the model's video enhancement capabilities from input to output. Experimental results utilize the RV1D dataset demonstrate that BasicVSR++ significantly outperforms the original BasicVSR and rival methods, with notable improvements seen when transferring from low-resolution to high-resolution inputs. Further results indicate that the proposed techniques contribute equally to the overall performance gains.

A precision vector boson scattering estimator is proposed for rapidly and accurately identifying the process with the goal of minimizing the sum of the time required and the deviation from the true value. Initially developed for high-energy hadron collisions, this method is now being tested for the first time at muon collisions with energy set to 3.8 TeV. The performance of the estimator is evaluated by comparing it to conventional approaches that rely on the transverse momentum of the lepton output, specifically $p_T^\ell$, and a multi-variate technique using Random Forests. Our proposed estimator demonstrates a significant improvement, reducing the root mean square error by approximately 25% relative to the $p_T^\ell$ method and approximately 15% in comparison to the Random Forest approach.

A model-based approach to reinforcement learning, where agents learn a separate dynamic model for each task, is investigated. However, combining a few general models with domain-specific models poses challenges due to increased complexity. To address this, an alternative framework is proposed where agents use an independent modular system to select a separate dynamic model for each task. Several modular system methods are evaluated, but most have significant limitations, such as requiring distinct connectivity patterns that hinder model efficiency. A novel fully-connected modular system is introduced, allowing all models to be accessed by all models modules. This innovative approach achieves superior performance compared to other methods not only for the proposed system but also for partially connected systems. Experimental results show significant improvements in model efficiency and performance using this innovative framework, such as a 2-task robotics reinforcement learning application where the proposed system reduces data requirements and enhances performance.

The construction of discrete approximations for the porous medium equation and a related type of equation over complete, non-compact metric measure spaces with a compact boundary will be demonstrated. These approximations are based on discrete Perona-Borgwardt-Kaisa type objectives. Additionally, the existence of a discrete analog to the Bismut-Caffarelli-Srikanth identity is proved for the PMHS type heat flow, enabling us to achieve compactness and thus, establish the convergence of the approximate solutions.

We present a fascinating argument within G\"odel's First Incompleteness Theorem that defies expectation. Let G(x, y) serve as the G\"odel-Rosser diagonal function, and let g(x) be a function that is representable within a sufficiently strong formal system n, with the property that for every input x, the output g(x) is greater than all values up to and including x. Let's suppose further that the function g(x) is also strictly monotonically increasing. Then, for any provable statement in n that for all inputs x, G(x, g(x)) represents False, there must exist unprovable truths within n of the form G(c, g(c)), where c is some specific input.

In Clifford analysis, an integral formula is established which resembles Hadamard's integral method, enabling the reconstruction of a function from its boundary values on a 3-dimensional surface, weighted by specific kernel elements. Consequently, a theoretical framework is derived which permits the determination of a function within a given domain, based on its eigenvalues and the values assumed on a separate, non-intersecting 3-dimensional surface.

This paper introduces a novel approach called Sequential Geographically Balanced Sampling (SeGBS) to select balanced sample points within a specified area. Building on GBS, SeGBS allows for an incremental increase in the sample size by adding more survey units over time, thereby enabling balanced sequential designs. A comparison between SGBS and SGAS shows that SGBS results in more evenly distributed samples when considering geospatial proximity.

Robust eye-in-hand calibration is crucial for ensuring that a camera accurately captures its surroundings, and traditionally requires time-consuming and expensive calibration tools or processes. In contrast, our method presents an uncalibrated approach that doesn't necessitate such tools, instead training a neural network to adjust the camera's internal parameters based on a single, randomly taken image. By leveraging a large dataset, our method trains a pre-trained network that can then be applied to calibrate an eye-in-hand camera system from any image, even one obtained from a different robot. Experimental results show our method yields smaller errors and a larger field of view compared to monocular methods, essentially providing a highly accurate, efficient, and universal calibration system for eye-in-hand cameras.

High-resolution spectral tomography is an inverse problem difficult to solve, especially when extracting flow velocities. Due to the ill-posed nature of this problem, a unique solution cannot be guaranteed. However, in medical imaging and flow tomography, it is assumed that images can be accurately reconstructed despite this uncertainty. Rather than providing a single answer, our approach generates multiple possible solutions, giving users a clearer understanding of the inherent ambiguity. We utilize a conditional generative adversarial network to create a distribution of high-resolution images that maximally informs a posteriori distribution, which is then sampled using the rejection method.

We analyze the stability of discrete dynamical systems of the form $X(n+1)=TX(n)$, where matrix $T$ and initial state vector $X_0$ exhibit specific rotational and scaling symmetries. Our investigation reveals conditions under which certain dynamically interesting invariant structures, which are flat across phase space and pass through the fixed point, cannot exist for integer or non-integer positive values of $T$.

Next-generation wireless networks will utilize terahertz frequencies to overcome rising data demands, yet their short range and signal propagation challenges necessitate the exploration of multi-hop routing. In this paper, we investigate terahertz multi-hop communication by assessing its potential and addressing certain limitations through an optimized beam training process. By formulating a problem that aims to maximize end-to-end throughput, we develop a reinforcement learning solution to simultaneously decide on optimal hop lengths and beam selections. Our approach is experimentally validated, and its benefits are illustrated through various scenario outcomes.

Located in the bright Scorpius-Centaurus stellar association, the L1-700 molecular outflow presents an interesting opportunity to study the interstellar medium. 
Using radio telescopes at 857 MHz, 432 MHz, and 330 MHz, researchers examined the interstellar medium along two paths. One path observed the L1-700 outflow directly, while the other observed it at an angle, providing a broader view. 
By analyzing scintillation patterns in data from the highly luminous pulsar B1133+16, they were able to detect variations in signal delay that could be attributed to changes in the interstellar medium. 
They found that along both paths, there was a significant correlation between scintillation patterns and signal delay at 432 MHz and 330 MHz, indicating a significant impact on the interstellar medium. 
However, along the second path, there was an additional component of the interstellar medium that was not along the line of sight to the pulsar, providing a broader view of the interstellar medium in this region. 
This study demonstrates the value of using scintillometry to study the interstellar medium in star forming regions, which could be further explored with observations of other bright pulsars in these regions.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limitations of WaveNet in generating speech using sample-based methods. QPNet, which is also a type of autoregressive generative model, addresses the inefficiency and lack of temporal understanding in WaveNet by employing a more suitable approximation method. This model is particularly effective for signals that have clear periodic patterns, such as speech, and is made up of specialized units organized into multiple networks. Each unit is responsible for predicting a specific phase of the waveform and incorporates external information, such as local pitch period and glottal relative pressure, through the dilated convolution neural network. Furthermore, QPNet demonstrates superior performance in speech synthesis, outperforming WaveNet in production speed while maintaining the same perceptual quality.

Researchers are using the James Webb Space Telescope to closely observe and track the photos and chemical compositions of temperate exoplanets, which may provide insights into planetary formation processes. To model what happens to light as it passes through planetary atmospheres, researchers have been using sophisticated numerical models for synthetic spectra. However, these models can be computationally expensive and difficult to apply in certain situations. This study presents a new semi-classical model for quickly calculating synthetic spectra in planetary atmospheres, which takes about 1000 times less time than previous methods. The new model was tested on the phase transition of methane from liquid to gas, which is relevant to the study of exoplanets like GJ 357 d. Additionally, the study introduces three open-source software tools to facilitate research on exoplanet atmospheres, which are now available for public use.

To differentiate between a Majorana peak and a pseudo-Majorana peak in a nanowire, we suggest utilizing tunneling spectroscopy with damping proportional to the resistance of the tunneling electrodes. By incorporating a tunable ferromagnet and balancing two conditions, a system can be achieved that is insulating yet possesses a pinned domain wall. Calculations of tunneling conductance, incorporating Tetrachannel Kondo (4CK) physics, show that the zero-bias peak of a true Majorana mode originates from the compressed domain wall itself.

The development of Urban Information Systems and Artificial Intelligence is accelerating the creation of a comprehensive urban database, often referred to as a digital twin. This project focuses on a groundbreaking approach to automatically identify and mark road issues, such as potholes and road markings, using image processing techniques in a swift and cost-effective manner. By leveraging this methodology, municipalities can efficiently create a comprehensive urban road dataset, enhancing their digital infrastructure. Specifically, this project demonstrates the capabilities of image processing through a public cloud system, providing access to a large-scale road dataset to research organizations through the RoadAtlas platform.

This study offers a detailed examination of the concept of shadows in higher-dimensional categories, along with associated ideas such as orthogonal track categories and semiorthogonal decompositions. We believe it will be valuable for understanding and potentially instructing readers on the nuances of such topics in a bicategorical context. Specifically, we aim to move beyond the limitations of 1-categorical descriptions found in existing literature, which we consider a significant shortcoming, and demonstrate how track categories provide a more accurate framework. Furthermore, this note incorporates elements of compactogenic track categories, as well as semiorthogonal decomposability within such contexts.

To precisely localize sound sources, traditional approaches rely on time difference of arrival, which we argue is inadequate due to the circular ambiguity it creates, as illustrated in the figure at the top center. Instead, a geometric approach using hyperbolas is required to effectively localize a sound source. The argument for this is supported by the observation that the time surface of ambiguity forms a cylindrical shape with circular cross-sections. Furthermore, to obtain a non-ambiguous (one-to-one) mapping between time and position, at least five microphones are needed, which appears unreasonable given human hearing with just two ears. Therefore, we conclude that the traditional approach is not sufficient to explain human auditory localization capabilities and argue that a geometric approach is essential for this purpose.

Recent years have seen a significant advancement in Graph Neural Networks, with their application in various fields. However, training these models requires labeled data, which is often expensive and time-consuming to acquire. To mitigate this issue, auto-encoders have been employed to adapt GNNs to unsupervised learning and graph classification, but they face a limitation in learning non-differentiable targets such as classification boundaries. To overcome this obstacle, we propose a novel approach called Lorentzian Graph Neural Networks (LoGNN), which allows for an unsupervised pre-training of GNNs, followed by a simple fine-tuning process to achieve a high performance in classification tasks. We achieve this by replacing the traditional Euclidean embedding space with a Lorentzian one, where the graph elements can be mapped coordinates that enable a graph optimization technique to position these elements to maximize cluster separation, thereby providing initial hidden states for the GNN. The result is high-performance outcomes from both low-dimensional and high-dimensional Lorentzian spaces, with the 2D and 5D variants of LoGNN outperforming the best performing GNN baselines on three classification datasets by 10%, 4%, and 3% respectively, on average.

This study focuses on a structural acoustic interaction, modeling the conditions when two bodies engage and interact as distinct entities before becoming a single unified body after collision. The research conditions cover two dimensions and three dimensions and incorporate rotational dynamics. For a given final state of structural acoustic interaction, the project endeavors to identify all possible initial configurations capable of producing the desired outcome, considering various scenarios arising from potential internal singularities that may form during the collision process.

Our research demonstrates that compressed light can be generated in a purely passive optomechanical setup by utilizing a pre-compressed mechanical oscillator. Within our model, the interaction between the optomechanical components results in a decoupling of their motion, ultimately allowing the production of an optomechanical state with negligible optical quadrature noise. This achievement is accomplished without requiring active feedback control systems.

We present an enhanced version of Prior's tree-based mu-calculus, which is expanded to include scalar and vectorial forms, catered to classical logic. A significant advantage of this modification is that it enables a natural derivation of the highest fixed-point operator from the lowest fixed-point operator and the negation operator. Furthermore, we demonstrate the equivalence between this enriched mu-calculus and a corresponding fragment of linear-time temporal logic that encompasses the star operator.

We present a novel efficient exponential (EE) utility function designed to accurately model efficient choice data from exponential delay discounting scenarios. This design aligns with previous efficient hyperbolic and power models but offers an alternative approach. Specifically, we incorporate the 2-tuple Tsallis entropy framework to create our novel EE model. Our findings demonstrate that our new Tsallis-efficient exponential (TEE) model outperforms hyperbolic, power, and traditional discounting models in accurately modeling choice data. We also discover that the TEE model implies the existence of negative value and entropy dissipation laws, resembling the negative heat equation.

In Substantial Gravity's Harmonic Gauge, the gravitational potential can be represented as a harmonic function of spatial coordinates and time. The concept of Harmonic Gauge has been explored, and the derivation of its conditions has been derived from first principles. The further conditions for selecting Harmonic Gauge could be predicted, and the correlation between these conditions could be analyzed from the field equations of Substantial Gravity. The framework of submanifolds in a four-dimensional manifold provides a unique prediction for these conditions, and these conditions are distinct from those proposed in General Relativity. The framework of submanifolds offers the possibility of describing physical fields using different submanifolds, and the derivation of the Harmonic Gauge conditions has been applied to two such submanifolds. The implications of these conditions on the consistency of the theory have been examined, and the potential for deriving the gravitational potential from the equations of Substantial Gravity has been further validated.

We investigate the concept of double covers of signed graphs, introducing novel notions like triple and quadruple double covers. A signed graph is considered to have a homomorphism limit if its quadruple double cover does an exhaustive search. If the quadruple double cover of a large enough signed graph does a superquadratic time homomorphism limit test, then its triple double cover can perform the same limit test. We demonstrate that this principle applies to specific graphs like complete graphs and their edge-subdivided versions. We also discovered an unexpected result: some quadruple double covers of signed graphs have a double cover that is itself a quadruple double cover of another signed graph. We introduced a new class of graphs called '2-2-expandable' and discovered numerous instances of such double covers.

The Weyl-Wigner representation has been employed to mathematically express and solve various quantum canonical equilibrium states, specifically those associated with Gibbs states, through a systematic and generalised canonical transformation. The notion of negative absolute temperature, initially introduced by W. Pauli, has historically been regarded as theoretical. In contrast, recent experiments have now given it a practical dimension. Although these achievements have been accomplished under highly controlled and unnatural conditions, we argue that the fundamental laws of thermodynamics can be applied to systems capable of negative absolute temperature.

UniToPatho is a comprehensive histological dataset consisting of 14,854 pairs of correlated whole slide images and corresponding hematoxylin and eosin stained images, all pertaining to colorectal polyps sections. This dataset, annotated by a consortium of pathologists, includes images with labels indicating the nature of the adenoma and dysplasia evaluation, including hyperplastic, tubular adenoma, p53-aberrant, low-grade dysplasia, high-grade dysplasia, and carcinoma labels. Currently, there is a significant lack of publicly accessible, annotated datasets of this scale, which hinders the advancement of histological AI methods, particularly in the tasks of polyp and adenoma-dysplasia evaluation. To rectify this gap, UniToPatho will facilitate research, evaluation, and improvement of machine learning approaches for complex histological tasks.

A novel computational method has been developed to tackle the high-frequency scattering of time-dependent waves from obstacles with complex shapes. This approach uses an adaptive discretization technique that independently handles the spatial and wavelength dimensions. By exploiting the non-stiff nature of the problem in a high-frequency context, any spatial dimension is manageable. The method employs different numerical methods in wavelength-scales to mitigate artificial scattering caused by discretization errors. A theoretical analysis has proven that this approach minimizes scattering errors at a optimal rate. The method is demonstrated with examples of acoustic and elastic scattering.

New measurements of the nowey2/100T/100H/100O ratios in Chelyabinsk and Benenitra meteorites match the ratios found in chondrules and CAIs from various meteorites that have landed naturally, as well as in the Earth's mantle and mantle-derived peridotites.  The data support the hypothesis that peridotites on Earth may originate from planetesimals with surfaces covered in water during formation.  Comparing the oxygen isotopic ratios of the meteorites to theoretical models suggests that peridotites on Earth formed through the collision of dry inner-core planetesimals and planetesimals in the outer solar system's water-rich regions.  Estimates suggest there were approximately $10^{8}$ water-covered outer core planetesimals between 3.0-3.5 AU during this time.  However, further analysis of the meteorites indicates that even inner-core planetesimals may have contained internally hydrated materials.  The findings also indicate that large, water-covered planetesimals played a significant role in forming the Earth's vast water reserves between 4.4-4.5 billion years ago.

Using a combination of integrable-to-integrable and coordinate-to-coordinate mappings, we establish comprehensive, analytically exact formulas for the n-particle form factors of the XXZ spin-1/2 chain's correlation functions, covering all distances. This analysis, conducted within the framework of affine quantum-algebra $U_q(\hat{{\mathfrak{s}}}{\mathfrak{l}}2)$ symmetry, leads to significant insights, including a deeper understanding of the model's spectral degeneracy. Furthermore, our findings suggest a potential universal structure for form factors that might apply to a broader class of solvable models.

Voice translation technology, particularly voice translation from one language to another, is crucial for enabling natural, cross-linguistic communication in services like telehealth, teleeducation, and business services. However, obtaining optimal performance in CT2G using shot-based models is hampered by slow training and model deployment. In response, we propose ZVT, the first zero-shot text-to-speaker neural translation system, and we provide evidence that speaker-adaptive models significantly outdo language-specific models in maintaining both accurate translation and consistent output. Furthermore, ZVT integrates existing, language-specific and speaker-adaptive models, and we show that it surpasses single-shot systems, offering improved production efficiency, a speedup of twelve times, in both computation and model size, while delivering comparable results.

To enhance optical simulations and scattering analyses of anemotropic figures, we developed a general technique for calculating multipolar moments. This method involves an exponential integral function and validates its efficacy by determining multipolar moments for various boundary shapes. We confirm its accuracy by comparing calculated results for circular and lemniscoidal boundaries with analytical solutions and observed discrepancies.

Altering the elementary symmetric functions by factorizing each term seems to yield functions with little relevance. However, when applying this concept to the Young symmetric functions, we encounter a more intriguing scenario. We've defined a new class of functions termed Schur altered symmetric functions, and have established a direct connection to the Schur Young bitableaux and the Schur Young symmetric functions. Furthermore, we've identified a less obvious connection between the Schur altered symmetric functions and the extended Schur symmetric functions developed by Orellana and Zelevinsky.

Within the most minimal scoto-Seesaw model, we examine dark matter consistency, the potential to detect it at colliders, and the stability of the electroweak vacuum. Neutrino masses within this model stem from type-II seesaw mechanisms, with right-handed neutrinos serving a dual purpose in generating these masses and providing a WIMP dark matter component. Using a refined potential, we assess the viability of the electroweak vacuum, and employ high-energy threshold techniques to simplify the calculation of neutrino stability. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of dark matter on the precision measurement of the vacuum. If certain conditions are met, we can ensure the stability of the vacuum up to very high energy scales, and potentially detect dark matter-nucleus interactions in experiments such as XENON1T.

The concept of bond formation between d and f electrons has been extensively studied for a couple of generations. Currently, researchers are examining how heavier, lighter transition metal electrons interact, specifically transition metals from groups 4 to 10. A key question remains regarding $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals located on adjacent heavy or light d-d electrons. Due to their different spatial distributions, these orbitals are typically classified as undergoing direct or mediated interactions. Nevertheless, our first-principles research indicates that $t_{2g}$ $e_g$ hybridization should be considered for both types of bonding. The results demonstrate that electrons in $t_{2g}$ $e_g$ orbitals are highly interconnected. Therefore, classifying heavy or light d-d electrons solely as direct partners or mediated interactions within pairs is misleading.

In this study, we extend the notion of twisted pair states to encompass Fock-Goncharov skew products for any unimodular variation, including birational maps. A key finding is that the resulting twisted pair algebras possess the property of being quotients of the original twisted pair algebras for their respective triangulations. Additionally, specific examples are provided to illustrate that twisted pair algebras for a single triangulation of a surface can be achieved through iterative deformation quantization of its classical limit torus components.

Deep learning techniques have achieved remarkable success in medical diagnosis,
particularly with input data preprocessed using transfer learning. However, such processing can
lead to altered semantic meanings and introduce inconsistencies between the physical features
visible in radiological images and known constraints, such as monotonicity and projectivity. To
address this issue, we have developed a novel loss function that considers image features
extracted from an encoder and incorporates information from chest X-ray annotations. This has
resulted in the creation of a new dataset, ICC-X, consisting of 11000 annotated images that
depict various cardiac pathologies. Furthermore, we propose a new loss function that considers
cardiac edge displacement, introducing a new dataset, ICC-X, consisting of 11000 annotated images
depicting a range of cardiac pathologies. Additionally, we have introduced a new loss function that
takes into account the semantic meaning and spatial location of displaced cardiac edges, leading to
improved model training and more accurate results.

ViDaExpert is an advanced tool that enables thorough visualization and analysis of multidimensional vector data. Developed using Python and Web technologies, it combines powerful computation with an intuitive, modern web interface. Researchers can seamlessly integrate large datasets, leveraging WebAssembly for efficient graph visualization and PETSc for accelerated numerical computation. As a result, ViDaExpert is an intuitive tool that enables thorough examination of complex phenomena, including mid-latitude atmospheric oscillations, through advanced visualization and integration of substantial datasets.

This paper employs graphical tools to quickly and intuitively evaluate Newtonian potentials on a flat, two-dimensional domain with a boundary, given any boundary conditions. These tools include graphs, vectors, and scalar fields, and are based on an efficient numerical algorithm using the Fast Multipole Method. We demonstrate that the proposed method is among the most accurate and computationally superior approaches, outperforming widely used alternatives, notably the method from Scipy.
